title: Reimagining lost panels: Malayali duo to complete 19th-century Cochin temple ceiling at London’s V&A
content: Held in storage at London's Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A) is a remarkable piece of South Indian architectural heritage: a 19th-century coffered wooden temple ceiling from Cochin. Spanning six metres by 1.7 metres, its surviving teak panels feature Hindu deities, each carved in a distinctive style. Of the original 45 panels, 25 are missing, leaving large gaps in a structure that has remained out of public view for more than seven decades. Now, the museum is turning to Malayali artist-and-designer duo Devi Seetharam and Ananth Ramaswamy to reimagine the missing sections. When the V&A's transformed South Asia Gallery opens in spring 2028, the ceiling will take centre stage, with 25 contemporary panels occupying the spaces left by the lost originals. "The ceiling was shipped from Cochin aboard the Banian in 1882. Architect and museum curator Sir Caspar Purdon Clarke purchased it during his expedition to India," Shannon Nash, Communications Manager at the V&A, told Onmanorama in an emailed response. Museum records from the period state that the ceilings came from a temple in Cochin that was demolished in 1874. The ceiling was last displayed in 1955 and has remained in storage ever since. It is now being conserved and reconstructed ahead of its return to public view. During the process, the museum found that several panels were missing and issued an open call inviting artists and designers to propose ways of reinterpreting the ceiling. Seetharam and Ramaswamy submitted a joint proposal and were selected after several rounds of evaluation. Having roots in Kerala gave us a basic, intuitive understanding of the artefact, says Seetharam. Her work Brothers, Fathers and Uncles, presented at the fifth edition of the Kochi-Muziris Biennale, explored patriarchy and men's dominance of public spaces through figures dressed in the traditional Kerala mundu. Reading the ceiling means something to us. There is an immediate recognition of the visual language, the way Kerala woodwork feels, the articulation of the deities on the surviving 20 panels. But our reinterpretation deliberately avoids representing those subjects directly. Instead, we are trying to create something that complements the ceiling without taking away from it in any way. That is something we are very sensitive about. Ramaswamy, founder of design studio Arall and creative director of his family's Bengaluru-based furniture business, Chester's, says the project is also about understanding how an object changes meaning when it moves between places and contexts. It's all about contextualisation. What does it mean that a ceiling from an Indian temple is now in a UK museum? Similarly, I am from Bengaluru, but I work in London. I'm constantly thinking about how we belong and where things belong, Ramaswamy told Onmanorama. The ceiling itself is a coffered ceiling with 45 panels, each of which would have depicted a deity. What has been particularly interesting is that they are carved in quite idiosyncratic ways. Each of the carvers involved in making the original ceiling had a unique mark and a unique way of carving. It appears to have been a group of different craftspeople rather than one person carving the entire ceiling, says Ramaswamy. Rather than recreating the missing deities, the 25 new panels will draw on the lotus, a recurring motif in Kerala's temple architecture. Characteristic of Kerala's architectural traditions, the coffered ceiling comprises a grid of square central panels framed by richly decorated beams. The longitudinal beams are carved with elephant corbel heads, while the transverse joists feature ornate lotus medallions. When you study the remaining panels, every deity sits within a rich landscape. There is ornamentation, jewellery, water, animals and floral garlands, says Ramaswamy. The lotus doesn't feel incongruous or unfamiliar. It sits quite sympathetically alongside the existing panels, he says...
